data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A panel of trained non-experts following a checklist will produce more reliable judgments because the panel's diversity (cognitive, demographic, background) acts as a noise-canceling mechanism for the checklist's inherent biases. The distinguishing evidence is that the panel's judgments will show lower variance across different checklists than the expert's judgments show across different framings of the same problem.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the panel is not sufficiently diverse, their errors will be correlated and will not cancel out.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the expert is trained to recognize and suppress their own biases, the panel's noise-canceling advantage disappears.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the checklist is biased in a way that aligns with the panel's common biases (e.g., a cultural bias), the panel will amplify, not cancel, the error.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"A checklist is a static model prone to systematic bias. A diverse panel applying it introduces idiosyncratic errors that are largely independent. By averaging or voting, the panel cancels out the non-systematic noise, isolating the checklist's signal. This is superior to an expert, whose intuition may contain systematic biases that are not cancelled out. Genuine reliability gain is shown if the panel's accuracy is robust to checklist imperfections, whereas mere compliance would make accuracy highly sensitive to checklist quality.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
